abstract: The extinct \textit{p}-process radionuclide $^{146}$Sm, decaying to $^{142}$Nd, is a key short-lived chronometer for the formation and early evolution of terrestrial planets and planetesimals. However, there has been a long-standing discrepancy in both the experimental measurements and the theoretical evaluations of the $^{146}$Sm half-life. To address this, a self-consistent microscopic framework for $\alpha$ decay is developed in this work, in which the $\alpha$ particle is treated as a four-nucleon quartet. Its formation amplitude in the nuclear interior is constructed from a coherent superposition of multiple pure single-particle configurations weighted by the pairing occupation amplitudes. Coupling this shell amplitude to the $\alpha$ cluster that survives in the low-density surface region yields a self-consistently determined two-state (shell~$\oplus$~cluster) preformation weight and effective potential. The calculated half-lives for the neighboring emitters of $^{146}$Sm are in good agreement with the measured values. Cross-validation over the neighboring emitters reproduces each excluded half-life without any nucleus-specific adjustment, and yields $^{146}$Sm predictions consistent to within $\pm 6\%$ of the resulting half-life $T_{1/2}=75.1^{+6.1}_{-5.6}$~Ma. This provides a solid calibration for theoretical studies of the early solar system.
hook: A new alpha-decay model puts the samarium-146 half-life at 75.1 million years.
summary: A new model treats the alpha particle as a four-nucleon quartet, joining a shell amplitude inside the nucleus with a cluster at the surface. Tested on neighboring emitters without per-nucleus tuning, it gives a 146Sm half-life of 75.1 Ma, good to about 6%. It is a theoretical prediction, not a new measurement, so it holds only as far as the model does.
title: Self-Consistent Microscopic Description of the 146Sm Half-Life for Early Solar System Chronology
